newsitem.title: ROMANIA: East European bourses unmoved by world news.
newsitem.headline: East European bourses unmoved by world news.

text.p: News of Rusian President Boris Yeltsin's successful surgery and Bill Clinton's re-election as U.S. president injected little glamour into East European stock exchanges this week.

Shares rose marginally in Warsaw after a surge in mid-week, Budapest saw mixed prices and Prague shares marked time. Prices rose in Bucharest and Ljubljana, while Zagreb was mixed. Bulgaria bourse remained closed pending legal procedures.

The Central European Share Index (CESI), which measures price movements of 73 selected Hungarian, Czech, Polish, Slovak and Slovenian stocks, closed at 1,405.81 points on Thursday, a scant 0.77 percent rise on the week.
WARSAW
Polish shares inched up after Wednesday's surge but analysts said selling after price-fixing signalled a fall on Friday followed by a horizontal trend.
Some analysts said investors might continue recent buying of large-cap stocks, heartened that the government might soon clear up disagreement on 1997 tax bills.

They welcomed the Senate legislative committee's rejection on Thursday of a tax cut for low earners proposed by the lower house last week that was seen as inflationary. The whole Senate votes on the issue next week.
The main market's all-share WIG index closed at 13,919.8 points, 421.9 points or 3.1 percent up from last Thursday's close before the All Saints Day holiday.
BUDAPEST
Prices traded mixed as the news of the successful operation of Boris Yeltsin and Clinton's reelection, as well as third-quarter results, failed to give a strong boost to the market.
On Thursday the BUX index closed at 3,632.74 points, up 18.54 points over last Friday.
Chemical company Borsodchem, hotel firm Danubius and home improvement product maker Graboplast hit all-time highs.
PRAGUE
Czech shares continued to stagnate and closed lower on Thursday after a modest gain to the PX50 in the previous session briefly kindled hopes of a long-awaited rebound on the Prague bourse.
Despite the generally gloomy mood among traders and analysts, some detected signs that demand may be gradually picking up.

Most activity on the bourse focused on major issues, especially SPT Telecom and Komercni Banka both of which released nine month financial results last week which were within the range of most analysts' expectations.
BRATISLAVA
Bratislava Stock Exchange saw another week of flat trading, with mostly small volumes traded in major issues.

The 12-share SAX index opened the week at 197.76 points, but its flat development was broken by a 8.26-point fall on Thursday. It closed at 190.32, due to huge losses in the heaviest issue of the bourse, oil refinery Slovnaft.
Slovnaft lost 90 crowns on Thursday, closing at 810, with brokers blaming the decline on the general downward trend on neighbouring markets.

The Slovak parliament on Wednesday approved an amendment to the securities law, which effectively allows issuers to cancel public trading of shares, or sell stakes in companies outside the official market.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks were mixed with hoteliers rebounding and blue-chip Pliva hitting a new high at 13,700 kuna. Fully-listed Zagrebacka Banka also dominated trading but eased to 1,015.
Traders said the market was beginning to recover with a return of foreign investors.
LJUBLJANA
Prices rose in Ljubljana, sending the SBI index up 10.60 points to 1,200.70. Total turnover was 1.2 billion tolars.
Bank SKB was the week's biggest gainer, firming nine percent, while financial consultancy Dadas was the leading decliner, falling 20 percent.
BUCHAREST
Most Bucharest shares edged higher but thin investor interest kept volumes low.
Overall turnover dived 21 million lei to 32.9 million on Thursday despite a newcomer to the market, private construction company Impact SA.
The VAB unofficial value-weighted index, computed by Vanguard SA securities, closed 1.7 percent higher from the previous session at 292.8 points.
BULGARIA

The Bulgarian stock market stayed closed for the third week in a row after the Bulgarian Securities and Stock Exchange Commision (SSEC) suspended stock trading on exchange floors until companies meet new legal requirements.
